blocks.text: 我们两人在 OpenAI 开始管理自己的团队时都才二十四岁。等你见到我们的团队，这一点就没那么令人印象深刻了。

blocks.text: 我们本该是干杂活的。二十四岁时，你处在公司阶梯的最底层。你做会议记录，写几份备忘录。经过多年枯燥的工作，你（但愿）会被授予更广泛的职权。

blocks.text: 我们的路径——以及当今许多年轻人的路径——看起来有所不同。我们进入职场时就已经有“员工”听命于我们。这些下属日夜工作，周末和节假日也不停歇。他们擅长干杂活。我们甚至还有数学奥林匹克金牌得主在团队中为我们提供建议。我们的新下属仍会犯下他们那份错误。但他们在变得更好，在学习我们的需求，而我们也在学习如何管理他们。

blocks.text: 当 AI 进入公司时，它会去哪里？我们提出三种示意性情景：

blocks.text: 在我们之下。每个人都保留自己的位置，而在下方生长出一层新的 AI 劳动力地下室。我们都成为管理者。我们先得到助手，然后是幕僚长，最终是整家微型公司向我們每个人汇报。每个人都获得晋升。

inlines.text: 在我们之下。
每个人都保留自己的位置，而在下方生长出一层新的 AI 劳动力地下室。我们都成为管理者。我们先得到助手，然后是幕僚长，最终是整家微型公司向我們每个人汇报。每个人都获得晋升。

blocks.text: 在我们身旁。AI 作为一种同事，与人们一起加入组织架构，直接为现有的人类管理者和高管工作。它一开始承担这项任务和那个角色。随着时间推移，它履行更广泛的职能，向更高的层级汇报。

inlines.text: 在我们身旁。
AI 作为一种同事，与人们一起加入组织架构，直接为现有的人类管理者和高管工作。它一开始承担这项任务和那个角色。随着时间推移，它履行更广泛的职能，向更高的层级汇报。

blocks.text: 在我们之间。最不直观的情况：上面是人，下面也是人，AI 在中间。它协调和监督工作，执行高管的愿景，同时认可有进取心的员工所做的独特贡献。

inlines.text: 在我们之间。

blocks.text: 这些情景都不会完全按照我们描述的方式发展，但我们认为三者都会以某种方式成真。三者都已经在以微妙的方式发生。

blocks.text: 我们在这里关注的不是完全自动化，而是转型中的经济。我们感兴趣的是，随着 AI 不断进步并融入现有组织，嵌合式公司会是什么样子。

blocks.text: 我们认为混合型公司在概念上很重要，因为 AI 的生产性采用并非一蹴而就。当模型只完成一部分任务时，由熟悉工作的基层员工来采用可能最容易。一旦模型能够端到端地执行广泛职能，高层就可以直接使用它们。在我们看来，能力更强的 AI 更容易被采用：公司必须学习技术，但劳动力会学习公司并能自我入职。

blocks.text: 我们的第一个情景似乎颠覆性最小。在这里，人们留在相同的座位上，保持相同的汇报关系，表面上做着和以前相同的工作。从今天到这个未来，人类的组织架构看起来没有变化。

blocks.text: 差异就在我们下方。在每一位个体贡献者之下，一支新的 AI 劳动力向每个人汇报。我们的组织架构图多出了一层地下室，而我们全都成了管理者。

blocks.text: 起初，这层地下室尚未完工。我们每人先带一两个智能体，它们算不上资深员工，更像是需要我们监督、也容易被我们宽容的 eager interns。我们的期望很低：在这里发封邮件，在那里起草份备忘录，到处回复 Slack 消息。就像初级人类员工一样，它们起步时自主权和信任都很少。

blocks.text: The two of us were twenty-four when we started managing our own teams here at OpenAI. That is less impressive once you meet our teams.

blocks.text: We’re supposed to be grunts. At twenty-four, you’re at the bottom of the corporate ladder. You take the meeting notes and write a few memos. After years of drudgerous work, you are (hopefully) granted a broader remit.

blocks.text: Our path—and the path of many young people today—is looking different. We enter the workforce already with “employees” at our behest. These deputies work day and night, weekends and holidays. They are great at the grunt work. We even have math olympiad gold medalists on staff to advise us. Our new reports still make their share of mistakes. But they are getting better, learning our needs, and we are learning how to manage them.

blocks.text: Our focus here isn’t total automation but a transitioning economy. We are interested in what chimeric firms will look like as AI improves and laces itself into existing organizations.

blocks.text: We believe the hybrid firm is conceptually important because productive adoption of AI isn’t instantaneous. When the models only do a subset of tasks, adoption may be easiest by ground-level employees familiar with the work. Once the models perform broad functions end-to-end, higher-ups can use them directly. In our view, more capable AI is more adoptable: firms must learn technologies, but labor learns the firm and can onboard itself.

Our expectations are low: send an email here, draft a memo there, reply to Slack messages everywhere. Like junior human employees, they begin with little autonomy and trust.

blocks.text: In our view, this “promoting” scenario still has much for junior workers to learn—judgment, taste, the muscles of management and creative vision. We will be incentivized to cultivate these skills because they show up in our work product. We will still learn by doing⁠(opens in a new window), but at a higher level of scope. Equity owners have different preferences than wage workers, because they reap the rewards⁠(opens in a new window) of harder work. The consultancy could enforce stricter adherence to specific regimens prescribed from the top.

blocks.text: Our view is, on net, workers will gain agency. Our optimism rests on firms using AI to flag consequential exceptions while leaving more decisions with workers.

blocks.text: We believe that AI will act as a scaffold—even if executives wish to maintain a coherent brand, this will merely be a constraint to operate within. Workers are made better aware of the business constraints at play and are better insured for creativity outside those restrictions. With their bases covered, execs can let employees try potentially lucrative new approaches. Aided by AI helpers beneath us, workers will also be responsible for more substantial outputs. We see more opportunities for creativity when commanding more complex work.

blocks.text: The same logic on worker autonomy also applies to firm size. Ronald Coase⁠(opens in a new window) asked why we organize production inside firms rather than through a web of contracts. Even an airplane could be constructed purely through peer-to-peer contracting, but it would be very inefficient. Firms muster economies of scale, align incentives, organize large projects, and absolve the need for constant bartering.

blocks.text: By easing communication, AI could justify larger or smaller firms. The classical firm is infrastructure for passing information up and instructions down, full of frictions and telephone-game. A larger firm (with more human employees) is less unwieldy if AI acts as a coordination layer. With the “AI consultancy,” an executive can know her firm the way a founder knows a twenty-person startup. She can watch an initiative’s implementation rather than await its quarterly retelling, and be pinged if anything happens. Her vision can infuse more broadly. Everyone is more aware of what everyone else is doing, and of the organization’s overall priorities.

blocks.text: A major motivation for vertical integration is to align incentives. There’s the idea of incomplete contracts⁠(opens in a new window)—an aerospace company could contract with a jet engine company, but for everything not explicitly required in the contract, the jet engine company is incentivized to cheap out and look after its own bottom line. To avoid this, the aerospace company buys the jet engine company. Just like with workers and bosses: if contracts are more monitorable and arbitrated intelligently rather than by checking off boxes, firms may be more comfortable relying on other firms. There would be less cause to do everything in-house.

blocks.text: We expect to see many smaller firms, but also sprawling AI “holding companies” where a huge number of different projects are conducted within one enterprise. The conglomerate is economical where there is some common asset leveraged by all the different projects. This common asset could be compute, though compute can easily be provisioned in small ad hoc quantities. A common factory or robot fleet is a better motivation.

An AI firm could avoid power struggles, share all information, and, where needed, instantiate creative diversity among its agents so that different paths are explored.

blocks.text: Today’s system is supposed to reward standout workers. They rise through the ranks and are better compensated. But in a world of superb model advisors, how will workers distinguish themselves?

blocks.text: What stands against this compression is judgment, taste, and scope. If we each lead AI firms beneath us, the residual human value is our decision-making. If each person is responsible for a larger effort under them, the difference between good judgment and bad rings louder⁠(opens in a new window).
